passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of three different dietary supplements on the resting metabolic rate (RMR) of healthy adults. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study enrolled 120 participants (30 per group). Participants were assigned to one of four groups: a placebo (Group P), supplement A (Group A), supplement B (Group B), or supplement C (Group C). After a 12-week intervention, RMR was measured using indirect calorimetry. Table 1 summarizes the mean RMR (kcal/day) and standard deviation for each group. The investigators hypothesized that supplements A and B would increase RMR relative to placebo, while supplement C would have no effect. The data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test. Results indicated significant differences between Groups A and P (p<0.01) and between Groups B and P (p<0.05), but no significant difference between Groups A and B (p=0.96). The authors concluded that both supplements A and B effectively increase RMR compared to placebo, with no superiority between them.
table_data:
Group | Mean RMR (kcal/day) | SD
Placebo | 1800 | 120
A | 1900 | 110
B | 1880 | 115
C | 1810 | 125
stem: Which group had the highest mean RMR?
explanation: Supplement A had the highest mean RMR (1900 kcal/day) compared to the other groups.
trap: Choosing the placebo or another supplement without comparing the means; Supplement A (1900 kcal/day) is highest.

stem: Which study design, as used here, best minimizes confounding from differences among participants (e.g., age or body composition)?
explanation: Correct: A) Random assignment spreads participant characteristics evenly across groups on average, minimizing confounding. Why the others are wrong: B) A cohort study observes self-selected exposures, so confounding remains. C) A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at one time without assignment. D) A case-control study selects by outcome and looks back at exposures, which is prone to confounding and recall bias.
trap: Choosing an observational design; only randomization controls participant variability and confounding.

stem: What is the approximate percent increase in mean RMR from placebo to supplement A?
explanation: Correct: (1900 - 1800)/1800 x 100 = 5.6%. Why the others are wrong: A) 2.8% is half the correct value. C) 5.3% divides by the supplement mean (100/1900) instead of the placebo mean. D) 11.1% doubles the correct value.
trap: Dividing the difference by the supplement A mean instead of the placebo (reference) mean.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the study results?

options.A: Both supplement A and supplement B produced significantly higher RMR than placebo.
options.B: The difference between supplements A and B was not statistically significant (p = 0.96).
options.C: Supplement A produced a significantly greater RMR than supplement B.
options.D: Supplement A's mean RMR exceeded the placebo mean by 100 kcal/day.

explanation: Correct: C) is unsupported; the A versus B comparison gave p = 0.96, so no significant difference was found. Why the others are wrong: A) A versus placebo had p < 0.01 and B versus placebo p < 0.05. B) This is exactly the reported result. D) 1900 - 1800 = 100 kcal/day.
trap: Treating the higher mean of A (1900 versus 1880) as a significant advantage over B.

stem: In this study, the placebo group (Group P) serves as which element of the experimental design?
explanation: Correct: The placebo group receives no active supplement and provides the baseline against which the supplement groups are compared, which is the role of a control group. Why the others are wrong: A) The independent variable is the supplement received, not a group. B) The dependent variable is the measured RMR. D) A confounder is an uncontrolled factor related to both exposure and outcome; the placebo group is included precisely to control for such effects.
trap: Choosing the independent variable because the placebo is one level of the supplement factor, when the group actually supplies the comparison baseline.
